content.text: I have what I need. The three families all sit under one superfamily in SCOPe 2.08, and I can now write the answer.

answers.answer:
SCOPe (current release 2.08, frozen 2021-07-28) classifies all three as members of the same superfamily, Cupredoxins (b.6.1, sunid 49503), within the Cupredoxin-like fold (b.6, sunid 49502) of class b (all-beta). They sit in three different families of that superfamily: Plastocyanin/azurin-like is family b.6.1.1 (sunid 49504); Ephrin ectodomain is family b.6.1.5 (sunid 74874; e.g. ephrin-A5, sunid 110105, mouse domains such as d1shwa_ and d2hleb_); and Peptidylarginine deiminase PAD4 N-terminal domain is family b.6.1.6 (sunid 110107; human domains such as d1wd8a2, residues A:4-112). The other PAD4 domains are classified elsewhere (middle domain b.2.9, catalytic C-terminal domain d.126.1.5), so only the N-terminal domain shares this relationship.

What this means at each level: placement in a common superfamily is SCOPe's statement that the three families are probably homologous, i.e. descended from a common ancestral Greek-key beta-sandwich (cupredoxin) domain, based on structural and functional features beyond mere fold similarity. Placement in different families means they lack the clear sequence similarity (roughly >30% identity or equivalent) that would indicate close evolutionary relationship, and that their functions have diverged. The shared fold (b.6) by itself would be the weakest statement, since fold similarity can arise by convergence; the superfamily assignment is stronger but still an inference of distant homology, not proof.

Should copper binding or electron transfer be inferred across them? No. Copper binding and electron transfer are properties of the plastocyanin/azurin-like family (b.6.1.1), where the type 1 copper site is formed by a specific His/Cys/His/Met (or similar) ligand set. Ephrin ectodomains (b.6.1.5) are cell-surface Eph-receptor ligands that mediate cell-cell signaling; they have no copper site and their cupredoxin-like beta-sandwich has been repurposed as a receptor-binding scaffold. The PAD4 N-terminal domain (b.6.1.6) is a non-catalytic immunoglobulin-like/cupredoxin-like domain of a calcium-dependent peptidylarginine deiminase; it does not bind copper and plays no electron-transfer role. Superfamily-level homology in SCOPe implies a shared ancestral fold and possibly ancient function, but function is frequently lost or changed across families within a superfamily, and the cupredoxin superfamily is a classic example of a scaffold recruited for non-redox roles (ephrins, PAD4, SAG1-type surface antigens in the sister superfamily b.6.2, etc.). Function transfer is therefore only defensible at the family level, and even then requires conservation of the specific copper-ligand residues.

Required external evidence before inferring metal binding or electron transfer in any new protein assigned to b.6.1: (1) structure-based alignment showing the type 1 copper ligand positions (His, Cys, His, Met/other) are conserved; (2) experimental evidence such as metal content/ICP or EPR/UV-vis spectra characteristic of a blue-copper site, or a crystal structure with bound copper; (3) sequence-level membership in the b.6.1.1 family (or another copper-binding family such as multidomain cupredoxins b.6.1.3) rather than only superfamily-level structural similarity. Template use for homology modeling of ephrin or PAD4 from plastocyanin/azurin (or vice versa) is reasonable for the core beta-sandwich only; loops, surface features, and any ligand site should not be modeled from a cross-family template. Representative selection should be done within the target family (e.g. ASTRAL representatives from b.6.1.5 for ephrins, b.6.1.6 for PAD4) and not from a different family in the superfamily.

answers.answer:
SCOPe (current release 2.08, frozen 2021-07-28) classifies all three as members of the same superfamily, Cupredoxins (b.6.1, sunid 49503), within the Cupredoxin-like fold (b.6, sunid 49502) of class b (all-beta). They sit in three different families of that superfamily: Plastocyanin/azurin-like is family b.6.1.1 (sunid 49504); Ephrin ectodomain is family b.6.1.5 (sunid 74874; e.g. ephrin-A5, sunid 110105, mouse domains such as d1shwa_ and d2hleb_); and Peptidylarginine deiminase PAD4 N-terminal domain is family b.6.1.6 (sunid 110107; human domains such as d1wd8a2, residues A:4-112). The other PAD4 domains are classified elsewhere (middle domain b.2.9, catalytic C-terminal domain d.126.1.5), so only the N-terminal domain shares this relationship.

What this means at each level: placement in a common superfamily is SCOPe's statement that the three families are probably homologous, i.e. descended from a common ancestral Greek-key beta-sandwich (cupredoxin) domain, based on structural and functional features beyond mere fold similarity. Placement in different families means they lack the clear sequence similarity (roughly >30% identity or equivalent) that would indicate close evolutionary relationship, and that their functions have diverged. The shared fold (b.6) by itself would be the weakest statement, since fold similarity can arise by convergence; the superfamily assignment is stronger but still an inference of distant homology, not proof.

Should copper binding or electron transfer be inferred across them? No. Copper binding and electron transfer are properties of the plastocyanin/azurin-like family (b.6.1.1), where the type 1 copper site is formed by a specific His/Cys/His/Met (or similar) ligand set. Ephrin ectodomains (b.6.1.5) are cell-surface Eph-receptor ligands that mediate cell-cell signaling; they have no copper site and their cupredoxin-like beta-sandwich has been repurposed as a receptor-binding scaffold. The PAD4 N-terminal domain (b.6.1.6) is a non-catalytic immunoglobulin-like/cupredoxin-like domain of a calcium-dependent peptidylarginine deiminase; it does not bind copper and plays no electron-transfer role. Superfamily-level homology in SCOPe implies a shared ancestral fold and possibly ancient function, but function is frequently lost or changed across families within a superfamily, and the cupredoxin superfamily is a classic example of a scaffold recruited for non-redox roles (ephrins, PAD4, SAG1-type surface antigens in the sister superfamily b.6.2, etc.). Function transfer is therefore only defensible at the family level, and even then requires conservation of the specific copper-ligand residues.

Required external evidence before inferring metal binding or electron transfer in any new protein assigned to b.6.1: (1) structure-based alignment showing the type 1 copper ligand positions (His, Cys, His, Met/other) are conserved; (2) experimental evidence such as metal content/ICP or EPR/UV-vis spectra characteristic of a blue-copper site, or a crystal structure with bound copper; (3) sequence-level membership in the b.6.1.1 family (or another copper-binding family such as multidomain cupredoxins b.6.1.3) rather than only superfamily-level structural similarity. Template use for homology modeling of ephrin or PAD4 from plastocyanin/azurin (or vice versa) is reasonable for the core beta-sandwich only; loops, surface features, and any ligand site should not be modeled from a cross-family template. Representative selection should be done within the target family (e.g. ASTRAL representatives from b.6.1.5 for ephrins, b.6.1.6 for PAD4) and not from a different family in the superfamily.
